newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Spotlight on East Timor with new bishop, visits.
newsitem.headline: Spotlight on East Timor with new bishop, visits.

text.p: The spotlight is on East Timor the next few days with the installation of a Catholic bishop on Wednesday and visits by a U.S. human rights official and a U.N. envoy to the territory annexed by Indonesia nearly 21 years ago.

Pope John Paul split the church administration of the former Portuguese colony late last year and named Bishop Basilio Do Nascimento to head the newly created diocese of Baucau covering the eastern end of East Timor.

The U.S. assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, John Shattuck, is due to visit Dili on Thursday and Friday. He will be followed over the weekend by U.N. special envoy Jamsheed Marker, diplomatic sources said.

The Roman Catholic administration in East Timor comes under the pope rather than being part of the Indonesian church establishment. Thus, papal nuncio Monseigneur Pietro Sambi, the Vatican's ambassador, will install the new bishop at a ceremony at Baucau on Wednesday.
The territory's other bishop, popular Nobel peace laureate Carlos Belo, has said dividing the diocese into two would not split the Timorese, but enhance their faith.
Reuters television correspondent Sarni Ocampo reported from the East Timor capital Dili that all was normal on Tuesday.
"There is no unusual activity, no extra security," he said.

Some diplomats in Jakarta said East Timorese might stage demonstrations over the next few days with the presence of more than two dozen journalists from foreign news organisations allowed by the government to cover the bishop's installation.
Indonesia invaded the territory on December 7, 1975, after civil war broke out following the withdrawal of Portuguese colonial authorities.
Jakarta incorporated it into Indonesia as its 27th province in July, 1976 in a move not recognised by the United Nations.

Indonesia has had a higher profile in the United States recently over human rights issues and donations to the Democratic Party election campaign fund last year by people close to the wealthy Indonesian Riady family.
Shattuck was also seeing several officials and non-governmental representatives in Jakarta, but diplomatic sources said the trip -- his first since 1995 -- was not unusual.
"There's been talk about a visit by him for some time, so it's not something that has been sprung on the Indonesians," one source said.
The U.N. special envoy has said he would decide how to proceed over East Timor after visiting Portugal and Indonesia.
He said in Lisbon earlier this month he was optimistic over negotiations between Portugal and Indonesia, which have dragged on for almost 15 years.
